column1995: I tried to offer what I thought was reasonable with the options I had. I didn't choose the $0 offer too often because I thought that if I offered any amount other than that, both parties would win. column1996: I was thinking I'd try to keep track of the player and what the previous card was at first but then I switched it to see if I could sense any type of pattern with the cards themselves. I was stubborn about keeping my guess as high even after a few in a row showed up as low. Then I tried to randomize how I guessed without keeping too much of a pattern myself. I pushed my luck a few times with guessing the same way a few times before switching to the other option.
column1997: For the doors, I picked whichever one was most pleasing to me aesthetically at first and then tried to use the feedback to see if I could detect a pattern. Also, for this questionnaire, I think it would be helpful to remind us who we played with during our games for when we wrote in our feedback. Also make sure you tell everyone to drink coffee before the scan so you don't fall asleep.

column1995: I trusted my friend to always split the money with me, so I always put the most amount of money on my friend. I was doubtful of the computer and the other partner. So, I would usually give the computer the least amount of money, except for when I just felt like taking a chance and giving it the full 8 dollars hoping to get a big return. For the other partner, I would give them 2 dollars, and if they gained my trust by sharing the money, I would give them up to 4 dollars. Then, if they shared the money, I would try to see how they would react with 8 dollars. If they shared the 8 dollars I would still trust them, but if not, they had to earn my trust back.
column1996: I just thought of the chances that a card that was higher than 5 or lower than 5 would appear based on the last recent cards. So, for example, if I had pulled three cards lower than 5 in a row, I would choose the next time higher just because I doubted the chances of another low one would still be there. Also, I would sometimes keep guessing the same thing (lower or higher depending on which one was right) if I got the same answer right two times. So, if I had guessed correctly two times that it was lower, I would keep guessing lower until it I got it wrong or I thought that it was too many in a row.
column1997: I usually just thought that the people who smiled the most would be the people who would be more likely to like me. Also, I would think that people with similar traits to me (similar skin tones or facial features) would also like me instead of someone who was more different to me. For the doors, I would imagine that I was on a quest and I had to choose between both doors to get a good or bad path. So, I would usually pick the one that looked cooler, more mysterious, or more intriguing as to what could be behind it. However, I also just tried to do a similar strategy as in the card guessing game where if the door on the right was the right answer too many times, I would go left because I would then imagine it couldn't be the answer anymore.
column1998: I just thought of getting the most amount of money, so I gravitated towards those amounts. I did decline money when I thought it was an offensive amount of money to offer. column1995: I committed myself to sharing the largest amount possible. As I was playing, the idea of committing to or contemplating sharing the smaller amounts seemed like a willingness to actively deny the other player out of spite (in response to them either keeping or sharing money in earlier decisions). That didn't really make sense to me and I instead made my decisions with a hope that I could help someone else and be mutually benefited.
column1996: I wrapped my head around having a 50% chance of success with each decision, though sometimes I caught myself behaving as if my past decisions were somehow capable of influencing the probability of the next selection ("The last time I selected 'lower', I was wrong, so it's more likely that selecting 'lower' the next time will be successful," etc.).
column1997: In the feedback game with the doors, it seemed like a true gamble. I wrapped my head around having a 50% chance of success with each decision, though sometimes I caught myself behaving as if my past decisions were somehow capable of influencing the probability of the next selection ("The last time I selected the left door, I was wrong, so it's more likely that selecting the left door the next time will be successful," etc.).    In the feedback game with the doors, it felt like a similar gamble, considering an individual's image offers me no prediction of their attitude towards my own image. Early on in the game, I began to make my decisions with a similar assumption that I had a 50% chance of selecting a face that liked me.
column1998: I committed myself to sharing the largest amount possible. As I was playing, the idea of committing to or contemplating sharing the smaller amounts seemed like a willingness to actively deny the other player for a chance of personal gain. That didn't really make sense to me and I instead made my decisions with a hope that I could help someone else and be mutually benefited.
column2012: I started to feel like I had the same likelihood of seeing a green check when selecting a face as when I was tasked with selecting a door.
column2020: I wonder if fatigue influences results. When each game first began, I felt strongly towards the decisions I made and the results of these decisions. Towards the end of each game, however, I felt significantly less excited/disappointed by the results of my decisions.
